Conversation field notes · July 2–11, 2026

Two small structures to keep handy

Across these 10 sessions, two specific error patterns recur in at least three sessions. Both concern the verb form after a familiar expression—not a need to make your conversation more formal.

Choose a focus below. Each has one optional application; you can switch at any time.

Focus 01 · Making a suggestion

Suggest that someone do something

Supported by 4 records across 4 distinct sessions.

From your session records
Original

She suggested me to take a break.

Revision

She suggested that I take a break.

Reusable rule

Name the person in a that-clause.

For a suggestion about an action, use suggest + that + subject + base verb: “suggested that I take.” Don’t use “suggested me to take” in this sense.

“She suggested” can stay. The repair is in what follows it. Here, I identifies the person taking the break.

Another option: suggest + -ing

Alternative revision of the source:
“She suggested taking a break.”

This names the proposed action but does not explicitly say who should take the break. Use “that I take” when you want to make that person clear.

You may also hear “She suggested that I should take a break.” That is a valid alternative.

Optional application · New teaching example

Report a colleague’s suggestion

Your colleague thinks you should ask for help. Choose the phrase that makes you the person asking.

“My colleague suggested ___ for help.”

Choose a completion

For your next conversation: “Someone suggested that I…”

Source trail · 4 records

The same original and revision shown above appear in all four records. Each is from a different session; these are repeated records, not four different sentence types.

Focus 02 · Talking about interests

Interested in learning

Supported by 3 records across 3 distinct sessions.

From your session records
Original

I am interested in learn more about plants.

Revision

I am interested in learning more about plants.

Reusable rule

After “interested in,” give an action the -ing form.

In is a preposition here. When a verb follows it directly, use the -ing form: “in learning,” not “in learn.”

“I am interested in” can stay. A noun also fits after it, as in “interested in plants.” Only a following verb needs this form change.

A correct form worth keeping: “to seeing”
Authentic source · Already correct

“I am looking forward to seeing you.”

Keep seeing. In “look forward to,” to is a preposition, so a following verb takes the -ing form. The supplied change to “see” is not a valid correction.

Sources: N04-U01 and N10-U01. These are correct uses, not additional errors supporting this focus.

Not every “to” works this way. In “I want to see you” (a new teaching example), to introduces an infinitive. Learn the expression, not a blanket rule about the word “to.”

Optional application · New teaching example

Mention something you want to explore

You’re talking about a possible new hobby.

“I’m interested in ___ my own vegetables.”

Choose a completion

For your next conversation: “I’m interested in learning more about…”

Source trail · 3 records

The original and revision shown above appear in each of these three sessions. The repeated evidence supports this specific “interested in” structure, not a claim that every -ing structure is difficult for you.

Why these two focuses—and not every suggested change?

A recurring pattern here needs support from at least three distinct sessions. Counts describe the supplied records, not how often an error occurs in all your speech.

The three past-tense errors occur in just one session (N06-U03, N06-U04, N06-U05). They are valid corrections, but do not establish a recurring pattern across sessions.

Other proposals change style or alter correct English. For example, “I think the plan is pretty good” is already grammatical (N01-U01, N07-U01). And “a little time” correctly means some available time; changing it to “little time” would change the intended meaning (N03-U01, N09-U01).

Keep the expressions handy, not a score. All practice is optional.
